title: Glasgow and London: Learning in Two Cities and Two Hospitals
paragraphs: I am 亀井温那, a sixth-year student in the Department of Medicine of the Nagoya University School of Medicine, and in 2025, through the clinical clerkship dispatch study abroad program, I experienced a total of eight weeks of clinical clerkship in the United Kingdom.

In this study abroad, I did clinical clerkships for four weeks in February in medical oncology at the University of Glasgow, a partner school, and for four weeks in March in pediatrics at St George's, University of London, a non-partner school. The learning at each university was very valuable and became an irreplaceable experience for me. Because there are two universities that looked after me, this will be long, but I report the content below.

I entered university in the midst of the confusion of the COVID-19 pandemic, and having heard at the guidance session that "there seems to be a medical English class," I, then a first-year who did not even know how to write an email properly, sent a clumsy email to Dr. Itzel saying I was interested. I can recall as if it were yesterday that she replied, "The class is stopped right now, so how do you even know the class exists? I'll contact you when there's a prospect of resuming." Starting from this, under the guidance of Dr. Itzel and wonderful seniors, I have enjoyed taking part in activities such as the medical English class and Clinical Case Discussion. In addition, through short-term study abroad and summer schools, I was blessed with opportunities to interact with students from other countries. Through these experiences, I witnessed that doctors and medical students in every region of the world are extremely diligent and excellent and work in medicine with pride in their respective lands. And my wish to learn and grow in a wider world gradually grew stronger.

Furthermore, as I came to have such an international perspective, I also became interested in the social and institutional aspects surrounding medicine and healthcare. I wanted to cultivate the ability to not merely learn reality as knowledge but to stand in the actual field and keep seeking better ways of medicine while continuing to view it critically. With that thought, I decided to take part in this dispatch study abroad program. Among countries, the United Kingdom has its own National Health Service (NHS), a healthcare system characterized by fairness, accessibility and being, in principle, free of charge. At the opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics the letters "NHS" were lit up, and in surveys on "what the British are most proud of" it is always ranked near the top, and the NHS is apparently special to the British people. Unfortunately, however, there is still no perfect system in the world, and the United Kingdom too is said to have various problems, starting with its biggest weakness, unstable funding, and strikes are frequent. I thought that learning under such a distinctive healthcare system would be very meaningful for me, who wanted to learn how the system affects the medical setting. Also, at the end of my third year of university I experienced a two-week short-term study abroad at the University of Cambridge. That was my first trip to Europe in my life, and I was strongly drawn to the charm of the United Kingdom, a country with a history and tradition outstanding even in the world and which has always remained a center of culture. This time I would be able to live and learn in that United Kingdom for two months, so my heart was pounding even before departure.

The University of Glasgow, founded in 1451, is the fourth oldest university in the English-speaking world after Oxford, Cambridge and St Andrews. Glasgow is the largest city in Scotland, and while it currently retains an aspect as an industrial city, it is also known as a city of culture and art. With many students and good public safety, and with tolerant and warm people, it was a comfortable city to live in.

I did a clerkship in medical oncology at the Beatson West of Scotland Cancer Centre, the second largest cancer center in the United Kingdom. Students of the University of Glasgow sometimes also rotate at Beatson for only one week, but it is reportedly so rare for an exchange student to come to Beatson that there may be one a year or none. For this reason, all the doctors taught me very enthusiastically simply because I was a student from Japan. Every doctor apologized with "Sorry we're busy," and I thought I must be grateful for being able to learn. Dr. Jeff, my supervisor, who leads Scotland's phase I clinical trials, prepared my clerkship schedule, and every day I could learn one-on-one under the doctor in charge.

What I spent the most time studying was the outpatient clinics. The outpatient clinics were wide-ranging and subdivided, covering colorectal cancer, upper gastrointestinal and hepatocellular carcinoma, gastroesophageal cancer, metastatic breast cancer, germ cell tumors, ovarian cancer, lung cancer, sarcoma, melanoma and phase I clinical trials. There were patients from new patients to those who had been treated for more than ten years, and sometimes an hour was spent on one patient. During consultations I learned how to deliver bad news, explain prognosis and present treatment options, and I was also given opportunities to ask patients questions and to assist with examinations, which was very educational. When I was first asked, with a wink, "What do you want to ask, Dr?", of course I was not mentally prepared, and since I was desperately trying to follow the already strongly accented English, I was taken aback, but I somehow squeezed out a question. As I got used to the clerkship I became able to communicate on my own, and I felt growth. Through the four-week clerkship, being able to follow a patient's course continuously, from the decision on treatment to dealing with side effects, was also a valuable experience.

I will introduce the learning that particularly impressed me from observing the outpatient clinics. There were many cases in which, although it was known to be stage 4 at the time of referral, the patient visited Beatson with it left vague, and was told "It's stage 4" for the first time at Beatson. The doctors at Beatson want to discuss treatment options with the patient, but for the patient, just receiving the announcement fills their head, and they cannot think as far as a discussion of the treatment plan. For that reason, one doctor lamented, "If the disclosure had already been done before they came to Beatson, we could have a more substantial discussion of the treatment plan." Many patients with so-called stage 4 for whom standard treatment did not work also gather at Beatson, but there were also many patients who, thanks to treatment at Beatson, kept their QOL for a surprisingly long time. For example, patients happily talked about holidays, such as where they had traveled and where they wanted to go, and treatment plans were made with flexibly adjusted drug-free periods to fit travel plans, so care was provided that stayed close to each individual's lifestyle. In the consulting room I saw patients talking with doctors with smiles many times. The people of Scotland love to chat, and there were many scenes in which they spoke to me proudly, saying "This doctor saved my life!" and "There's no doctor as wonderful as this!" The doctors often used the expression "We can't Cure your cancer, but we can Treat it." Seeing cancer patients living vividly thanks to treatment at Beatson, I felt the importance of, and a sense of mission in, constantly pursuing the development of new treatments. I also gained the important learning that the relationship of trust with patients and dialogue that becomes a mental support are themselves part of treatment.

Besides observing outpatient clinics, there were many other learning opportunities. At the Acute Oncology Assessment Unit (AOAU), I did the initial response to cancer patients needing emergency care through the Helpline. As in general emergency care, doing the medical interview and physical examination and, based on the results, summarizing in a paper chart while discussing with a doctor was very practical. At the Pharmacy, I learned that as a clinical trial site it handles 400 to 600 protocols, of which 150 trials are active. As a medical student I had had opportunities for interprofessional education before, but being able to learn about drug management and the progress of trials from a pharmacist's viewpoint was very meaningful. I was also given the opportunity for GP clerkships at an outside hospital and with Dr. Alec, who has looked after me for many years, and could compare them with the learning at Beatson.

I could glimpse the character of the United Kingdom everywhere. For example, imaging reports take about a week and PET examinations about six weeks, which is unthinkably long in Japan. In exchange, I saw devices such as substituting telephone consultations if there is no problem. There is a Nurse Practitioner specializing in ages 16 to 26, and I felt the professionalism of covering a niche but certainly important aspect within a cancer center with many elderly patients. The café in the hospital is run by a Cancer Charity, and even a free coffee wagon service circulating through the hospital is provided, and I felt the culture of donation firsthand. Doctors are not on a shift system and all go on Holiday at once, so there were weeks of staff shortage. Also, in Scotland, famous even within the United Kingdom for whisky and deep fried food, there are many diseases caused by lifestyle; for example, hepatocellular carcinoma is overwhelmingly caused by alcohol and obesity rather than by viral infection, which is predominant in Asia, and there were conspicuous patients with hereditary hemochromatosis, common in Celtic people, and Dr. Jeff said with a wry smile, "I never saw a single one in Japan, and today we've seen three."

Between clerkships I was also blessed with various opportunities for interaction. I had been in contact before departure with two students who had come to Nagoya University Hospital the previous summer, and I was able to meet them again locally and spend enjoyable time. My Student Buddy contacted me many times out of concern for me. I was also able to talk with Glasgow University students rotating at Beatson about the intercalated year and the British doctors' training system. For example, I learned that the initial residency placement is decided entirely at random in order to distribute medical students fairly, and that obtaining specialist qualification takes longer than in Japan. Since the University of Glasgow itself is a comprehensive university, after the clerkship I joined club activities in which students of other faculties also took part, and was soothed by the majestic and beautiful campus reminiscent of the world of Harry Potter. In addition, Dr. Alec took me to my first opera and orchestra in my life and even to the Glasgow Film Festival, and I was able to make many unforgettable memories.

St George's, University of London, founded in 1733, is the second oldest public medical school in the United Kingdom. It is in a district of London called Tooting. Tooting is east of Wimbledon, an upscale residential area, and is reportedly the hometown of the current Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan. With many immigrants of Indian and Pakistani origin, it was a lively town full of diversity, with a downtown atmosphere as well.

I did a pediatrics clerkship at St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. It is an acute general hospital with more than 1,300 beds, slightly more than Nagoya University Hospital, and being attached to the university, it has an environment in which one can learn lectures and practice seamlessly. As features of pediatrics, there is a PICU, which only limited hospitals in London have, and infectious diseases is especially famous, with a team specializing in pediatric infectious diseases. Dr. Jane, my supervisor, arranged the clerkship schedule according to my wishes, and in addition to the daily handover and teaching, roughly in the first week I did the ward, in the second week the outpatient clinic, in the third week neonatology, and in the fourth week the infectious diseases team. Besides that, I was also allowed to observe the hospital's own initiative, the "Blue Sky Unit," where patients can be seen without waiting, and the PICU.

I will introduce the learning that left an impression. On ward rounds, for new patients, a system was in place in which a Consultant always accompanied and rounds were done as a team. One Consultant said, "Worried parents want a 'label' in the form of a diagnosis, but rather than easily giving a label, it is important to carefully carry out the necessary exclusion diagnoses." What especially impressed me in the pediatric specialty outpatient clinic was the attitude of always "first listening to the child," while adjusting to the developmental stage. Starting by confirming the age, they eased the child's tension with chat such as "Who did you come with today?" and "How's school?", and then moved naturally to the medical interview through the question "Why do you think you came to the hospital today?" For me, who had gotten used to the style in which the parent mainly talks, seeing a child of about five speaking up clearly about their own allergy was very fresh and shocking. One impressive case was a three-year-old Somali boy referred with a chief complaint of vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain two to three times a month. Because language interpretation was needed, the consultation was conducted using telephone interpretation. Through an interpreter the consultation takes time, but as a result of persistent history taking, the cause was that the parents gave too much junk food. The doctor in charge said that because the time GPs can spend on history and physical examination is too short, children whose diseases should be diagnosable by history and examination in 90% of cases are being referred to specialists, that this is one factor in the long waiting times for specialists, and called the British healthcare system a "broken system." In neonatology, they sometimes prefaced with "I think Japan is more advanced in this, though," or asked, "The person who taught me NAVA is a Japanese doctor, Dr. ○○, do you know him?", and I reaffirmed that Japanese neonatology is highly evaluated worldwide. The infectious diseases team takes consultations from each department and is in charge of infection management and planning antibiotic treatment, and I was able to experience a part of the training specializing in infectious diseases, which is its strength.

Handover and teaching were, overall, very full. In the pediatric emergency teaching, simulators were used, with roles of resident, trainee and supervising doctor played and SBAR-style handover incorporated, and after each simulation everyone reflected together, a format of deep learning emphasizing communication. In pediatrics teaching, differences in communication styles by race were sometimes the theme. For example, the content was that white patients tend to actively object to and ask questions about the opinions of healthcare professionals, whereas non-white patients tend not to show their doubts or anxieties and to answer "Yes" even when they do not understand. Such a viewpoint is not much discussed in Japan, and I found it very interesting. Also, every Thursday noon there was an optional lecture called "Ground Round," which was a place of interaction across departments. When I took part, a nephrology lecture was given as part of a World Kidney Day event, and there was also a discussion on "clinical ethics," about a case concerning emergency blood transfusion for a pregnant woman and religious restrictions. In addition, research presentations by research fellows were also held, and I could deepen my learning from diverse viewpoints.

Between clerkships I was also blessed with various opportunities for interaction. In the dormitory the university provided, I encouraged my flatmates about each other's clerkships and exams and also took part in events organized by students belonging to the dormitory. Invited by my flatmates, I, who do not usually draw, took on sketching for the first time since anatomy practice, and spending a Saturday morning leisurely in a beautiful London museum was a very rich time. Also, what was especially impressive in conversations with students during the pediatrics clerkship was the story that "an acquaintance suffered severe pain from a urinary tract infection but could not get medication prescribed easily and ended up returning to their home country, India," and the reality of "a two-year wait for surgery for external hemorrhoids." It was an opportunity to learn realistically, in conversations among students, about such challenges of access to medical care. Furthermore, I spent the four-week clerkship together with an Italian student who was studying abroad through the Erasmus program and aspired to pediatric endocrinology. Because it was a one-on-one teaching format, we often acted separately during the clerkship, but we matched our lunch times and talked about each other's countries' medicine and culture, and on weekends we sightsaw in London together, and we built a deep friendship.

I accumulated valuable experiences in terms of learning. First, being able to do clerkships in contrasting regions, even within the same United Kingdom, Glasgow, which many large patients with strong Scottish accents visit, and London, where patients with diverse cultural backgrounds gather and multilingual response is required, was a great learning. Furthermore, being able to place myself in medical settings at different levels, Primary care (GP surgery), Secondary care (St George's Hospital) and Tertiary care (Beatson Cancer Centre), deepened my understanding of the British healthcare system even more. Through these experiences I could feel firsthand the influence of the system on the field, and it also became an opportunity to look anew at the Japanese healthcare system. Also, fortunately, I was blessed with opportunities to visit Francis House, a children's hospice in Manchester, England, and the Princess Máxima Center, a cutting-edge center for pediatric cancer research in Utrecht, the Netherlands. I was able to think deeply about the shape of whole-person care that stays close to each patient and about the significance of contributing to the future of medicine through research.

Life abroad gave me various opportunities for challenge. As one example, I do classical ballet, and since I had a recital coming up in the summer, even during my study abroad I looked for a local studio on my own and took part in open classes. Because I normally live with my parents, it was my first time living alone, and continuing ballet lessons alongside the clinical clerkship in an unfamiliar foreign country was not easy, but I was able to continue without slowing the pace of lessons I have in Japan. Dancing with dancers from various backgrounds was a great stimulus, and I could feel technical improvement, which led to confidence. Meeting many new friends through ballet was also an irreplaceable experience for me.

Finally, I was able to realize this study abroad thanks to so many people that I cannot write them all: Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. Branko, who gave me this valuable opportunity for study abroad, Dr. 柴原, who gave great support in the form of a fund, Dr. Itzel, who has guided me warmly and strongly since my first year, Dr. 長谷川, who gave great support with applications and procedures to multiple schools, Mr./Ms. 宮川, who made efforts with the scholarship program procedures, the doctors of the Frontier Society, who passed on the baton of this dispatch study abroad program, including guidance in the form of pre-departure training, Dr. Jeff of the University of Glasgow and Dr. Jane of St George's, University of London, who took on the role of supervisor, the doctors of Nagoya University pediatrics and obstetrics and gynecology, who warmly watched over me before and after my study abroad, and my parents, who are my treasure at all times. I take this opportunity to express my deep gratitude from my heart.
I will surely make use of the valuable experiences gained through this dispatch study abroad program in the future.
